newsitem.title: DUBAI: King Fahd says Saudi economy much stronger.
newsitem.headline: King Fahd says Saudi economy much stronger.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's King Fahd said the kingdom's economy was much stronger than the world thought despite low oil prices in recent years and the burdens of financing the Gulf War that ended Iraq's occupation of Kuwait.
King Fahd made his remarks in his annual address to the consultative Shura Council, which ended early on Thursday.

"You know the events that hit the region in the past years that exhausted our economy and development, but despite that we remained...strong. Our economy is much stronger than others imagine," the official Saudi Press Agency quoted the king saing.

Saudi Arabia's role in ending Iraq's seven-month occupation of neighbouring Kuwait in 1990-91 cost it an estimated $50 billion which put a huge strain on its economy, already hurting from low oil prices that improved only in 1996.

"Our industry is developing day after day. In the past years we imported many of our needs, but today our industry has developed and our factories are in the thousands producing thousands of different kinds of basic commodities," he said.

Saudi Arabia said this month that loans extended by the state Saudi Industrial Development Fund (SIDF), which plays an important role in efforts to encourage the private sector, rose 21 percent in 1996. It put industrial growth in 1996 at nine percent, up from, 7.5 percent in 1995.
The king said one of the government's priorities was developing the industrial and agricultural sectors to achieve greater economic security for the world's largest oil producer and exporter.
The king did not make any mention in his speech of remarks he made in an interview earlier this month in which he said the kingdom was examining political reforms introduced in 1993.

King Fahd in 1993 set up the 60-member Shura Council, the kingdom's first representative body for almost 60 years, and set up regional assemblies in 13 provinces, the first steps towards giving Saudis more say in running the country's affairs.
